subject: Attention sink formation dynamics and their downstream effects on key-value cache eviction strategies in long-context inference

Topic: Attention sink formation dynamics and their downstream effects on key-value cache eviction strategies in long-context inference

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1480)
response:
Attention sinks are a small set of tokens — typically the first one or two positions in a sequence — that accumulate disproportionately large attention scores across nearly all heads and layers, not because they carry semantic weight but because softmax must distribute probability mass somewhere even when no token is genuinely relevant. The central question is: if you're running long-context inference with a compressed KV cache (evicting entries to stay within memory budget), how do you handle these sink tokens correctly, and what goes wrong if you don't? The key concepts in play are: softmax's partition-function behavior forcing attention scores to sum to 1, the resulting "sink" phenomenon documented empirically in models like LLaMA, KV cache eviction policies (recency-based, attention-score-based, hybrid), and the interaction between eviction decisions made at layer l and the representational damage that propagates through layers l+1...L. What a beginner misses is that evicting a sink token doesn't just lose one token's value vector — it destabilizes the attention distribution globally for every subsequent token in every subsequent layer, because heads that were offloading their "nowhere-to-attend" probability mass to that sink now redistribute it onto semantically meaningful tokens, silently corrupting their representations without any obvious error signal. The expert also worries about a subtler second-order effect: attention-score-based eviction policies are biased toward retaining sinks (they look important by score), which means under memory pressure you may be protecting semantically empty positions at the cost of evicting genuinely informative middle-context tokens.

NEXT: If attention-score magnitude is an unreliable signal for eviction because sinks inflate it artificially, what alternative signals or proxy metrics could actually distinguish a token that is load-bearing in meaning from one that is merely load-bearing in the softmax partition?

The most direct alternative is to measure a token's value-vector contribution to downstream residual stream updates — specifically, the L2 norm of the weighted value vector (attention weight × value vector) summed across heads, which H2O (Zhang et al., 2023) partially exploits but conflates with raw score. A cleaner signal is gradient-based importance: how much does the loss change if this token's KV entry is zeroed? This is expensive online but has been approximated cheaply via first-order Taylor expansion in pruning literature (Michel et al., 2019 on head pruning), and the same logic applies per-token. Retrieval frequency across layers is another proxy — SnapKV (Li et al., 2024) tracks which tokens receive high attention consistently across multiple layers, not just in one head at one layer, filtering out sink inflation because sinks tend to dominate shallowly rather than being selectively retrieved deep in the network where semantic composition happens. Positional entropy of attention distributions offers a complementary diagnostic: a head that is genuinely using a token shows low-entropy, targeted attention; a sink-loading head shows diffuse redistribution the moment the sink is removed, which you can detect by comparing per-head entropy before and after candidate eviction. The practical worry experts have with all of these is measurement cost at inference time — gradient signals require a backward pass you don't have, cross-layer tracking requires buffering statistics across forward passes, and the whole point of KV eviction is to save memory and compute, so your eviction oracle can't cost more than the cache it's managing.

The canonical failure mode is topic drift invalidating the eviction profile: if a long-context document starts with legal boilerplate and then asks the model to reason about a technical clause buried at position 8,000, a prefill-phase eviction policy that saw mostly uniform attention over the boilerplate will have discarded the clause's KV entries before the generation phase ever issues queries that would have retrieved them — the token is gone and unrecoverable. This is not hypothetical; InfLLM (Xiao et al., 2024) explicitly motivates its streaming block-retrieval design around this failure, showing that fixed eviction baselines degrade sharply on multi-hop reasoning tasks where early prefill attention is a poor proxy for what generation-phase queries actually need. A second failure mode is query-type phase transitions: a model generating a summary behaves differently from one generating a follow-up answer to a user question in the same context window, and the attention sink structure itself can shift — heads that were sinks during summarization become task-relevant during QA, meaning your eviction decisions were calibrated to the wrong regime. Third, speculative and multi-turn inference compound this: in multi-turn dialogue, each new user turn introduces a query distribution the prefill phase of turn 1 had no signal about, yet the KV cache from turn 1 has already been pruned, making the system structurally unable to retrieve context that only becomes relevant three turns later. The deeper expert concern is that static eviction implicitly assumes query-key relevance is frontloaded and stable, which holds reasonably for single-turn extractive QA but breaks badly for agentic, multi-step, or instructed-reasoning workloads where the model's own generation creates new retrieval needs that didn't exist at prefill time.

The asymmetry is real and already implicit in how systems like PagedAttention (vLLM) physically separate prompt and generation phases, but almost no eviction policy exploits it semantically — they treat all KV entries as a flat pool ranked by the same score. The case for differential treatment is strong: prompt tokens have fixed keys and values determined at prefill, so their eviction impact can in principle be estimated once; generated tokens, by contrast, have keys and values that were themselves conditioned on a partially-evicted cache, meaning their representations carry compounded approximation error that makes their eviction cost harder to estimate and potentially higher. A concrete architectural change this demands is provenance tagging — each KV entry annotated with whether it was prompt-derived or generation-derived, plus optionally which cache state it was computed under, so eviction policies can apply asymmetric retention budgets; Pensieve (2024) gestures at cache lineage tracking but doesn't fully implement generation-versus-prompt asymmetry. On the systems side, treating generated tokens as higher-volatility entries suggests a two-tier cache: a protected prompt cache (potentially offloaded to CPU/NVMe but never evicted, as in llama.cpp's prompt caching) and a smaller, actively-managed generation cache subject to rolling eviction with shorter retention horizons. The harder architectural implication is that RoPE positional encodings complicate reuse: because keys are position-encoded at write time, a generated token's KV entry is only valid at its original sequence position, so any system that wants to reorganize or selectively retain generated-token cache entries must either recompute positions or accept that cache entries are non-transferable across sequence rearrangements — a constraint that essentially rules out certain classes of dynamic cache reorganization that work fine for prompt tokens.

When a draft token at position p is rejected in speculative decoding, the KV entries computed for it — and for all subsequent draft tokens that were conditioned on it — must be discarded entirely, not recycled, because their keys embed RoPE frequencies for positions that will now be occupied by different tokens with different semantic content; systems like Medusa and SpecInfer handle this by maintaining a rollback pointer that truncates the KV cache to the last verified position, which is cheap (just moving a pointer in PagedAttention's block table) but means every rejected draft token represents wasted KV computation proportional to the draft length. The interaction becomes dangerous under tree-based speculative decoding (as in SpecTree or Eagle-2), where multiple draft continuations are evaluated in parallel as a token tree — each branch occupies a distinct position range, and the KV cache must simultaneously hold entries for mutually inconsistent futures; Eagle-2 reports draft acceptance rates around 80-90% on coding tasks, meaning 10-20% of KV computation per step is structurally guaranteed to be discarded, and this waste scales with tree width. The deeper problem is that attention sink dynamics shift under speculative execution: the draft model (often a smaller, distilled network) may produce different sink token distributions than the target model, so the KV entries it generates for non-sink positions are computed against a different effective attention partition than the target model would have used, introducing subtle representation mismatch even for accepted draft tokens' values. A systems change this motivates is lazy KV materialization for draft tokens — deferring full KV write until acceptance verification, storing only the logits and token identity during drafting and recomputing KV only for accepted tokens; this trades latency for memory bandwidth but requires the verification pass to be KV-cache-aware in a way current implementations (which separate draft and verify passes cleanly) are not. The sharpest unresolved tension is that speculative decoding's speedup depends on long accepted runs, but long accepted runs from a draft model with different sink structure silently accumulate KV entries whose positional and distributional provenance differs from what a non-speculative target model would have written — a form of cache poisoning by proxy model that has no current detection or correction mechanism.

The case for an explicit sink-alignment objective is strong but the right target distribution is non-obvious: naively minimizing KL divergence between draft and target attention weight distributions at sink positions would just teach the draft model to replicate the target's softmax partition, which doesn't actually ensure the value-weighted outputs (the quantity that matters for residual stream updates) agree — you need to match weighted value projections (∑ α_i v_i) layer-by-layer, not raw attention weights. Eagle-2's distillation already minimizes feature-level distance between draft and target hidden states, which implicitly constrains sink behavior, but it does so at the output of each layer rather than decomposing the contribution of sink tokens specifically, meaning sink misalignment can be masked by compensating errors elsewhere in the layer that only manifest at longer contexts. A cleaner objective would be a sink-conditioned feature matching loss: identify the top-k sink positions under the target model, then penalize the draft model when its value-weighted output excluding those positions diverges from the target's — this isolates whether the draft model is using sinks as a load-bearing softmax dump the same way the target does, rather than distributing that probability mass onto semantically meaningful tokens. The practical difficulty is that sink positions are context-dependent and not fixed at training time — position 0 is reliably a sink, but secondary sinks (newline tokens, delimiter tokens, BOS-adjacent tokens) shift with domain, so the alignment objective needs either a dynamic sink-detection subroutine during training or a learned sink-position predictor, both of which add non-trivial complexity to the distillation pipeline. What makes this especially sharp is that current speculative decoding evaluations benchmark on acceptance rate and wall-clock speedup, neither of which directly measures KV distribution fidelity — a draft model could achieve 85% acceptance rate while systematically miscalibrating sink structure in ways that only corrupt outputs on long-context multi-hop tasks, meaning the standard eval suite would give no warning signal.

Fine-tuning on a narrow domain demonstrably shifts attention patterns — studies on instruction-tuned versus base LLaMA variants show that RLHF and supervised fine-tuning alter layer-wise attention entropy significantly, and since sink formation is a consequence of how specific heads learn to handle "nowhere-to-attend" probability mass, a coding-specialized fine-tune that rarely sees conversational openers will likely develop different secondary sink positions than a chat-tuned variant even if both share identical base weights. The implication for prefix caching (as implemented in vLLM's automatic prefix caching or SGLang's RadixAttention) is subtle but serious: prefix cache hits are validated by token identity and position, not by attention topology, so a shared system prompt cached under the base model's KV computation will be silently reused by a fine-tuned variant whose sink structure assigns different attention weights to those exact tokens — the cache entry is positionally valid but distributionally stale. This matters most at adapter boundaries in LoRA-served multi-tenant systems: when vLLM or similar systems serve multiple LoRA adapters on top of shared base weights, the base layer KV entries for a shared prefix are computed once and reused across adapters, but each adapter's attention projection matrices (Q, K in LoRA configurations that touch attention) will interact with those cached K entries differently, potentially routing sink-destined probability mass onto semantically loaded tokens in one adapter while correctly dumping it on position 0 in another. A concrete failure scenario is a system prompt prefix — say a 512-token instruction block — cached from a general assistant fine-tune and then served to a legal-domain fine-tune; the legal model's heads may have learned that certain structural tokens (section markers, "whereas" clauses) function as secondary sinks, but those tokens' KV entries in the cache were computed without that learned bias, so the legal model's attention effectively operates against a mismatched key distribution for every generation step. The expert-level concern this raises for multi-tenant inference infrastructure is that cache hit rate, the primary efficiency metric for prefix caching, is actively anti-correlated with distributional correctness when adapter sink topologies diverge — the more aggressively you cache, the more silently wrong your KV entries become across adapter boundaries, with no runtime signal distinguishing a correct cache hit from a topology-mismatched one.

A theoretically complete invalidation criterion would measure expected residual stream divergence — the L2 distance between the hidden states the current adapter would produce by recomputing the prefix versus what the cached KV entries will induce during attention, integrated across all layers — but this requires a forward pass over the prefix, which defeats caching entirely. The tractable proxy direction that avoids full recomputation is adapter-conditioned key distribution fingerprinting: at cache-write time, record a low-dimensional sketch (e.g., a random projection of the mean and variance of key vectors at each layer) tagged to the writing adapter; at cache-read time, the incoming adapter computes the same sketch on a small sentinel set of tokens — perhaps just the first 16-32 tokens of the prefix, which are disproportionately likely to include sink positions — and invalidates if cosine distance between sketches exceeds a calibrated threshold. The sentinel-token approach is motivated by the fact that sink topology divergence manifests earliest and most strongly at low positions, so checking only the first 16 tokens' key distribution gives you a cheap early-warning signal without scanning the full prefix; the compute cost is O(16 × d_model) per cache read, which is negligible relative to a cache miss that would require recomputing hundreds or thousands of tokens. A complementary approach is per-adapter sink-position registries: during adapter fine-tuning or a brief calibration pass, identify the top-3 sink positions empirically across a representative sample, store them as adapter metadata, and at cache-read time flag any cache entry where the writing adapter's registered sinks don't intersect with the reading adapter's — this is O(1) lookup with no runtime computation, though it requires the calibration infrastructure and fails for adapters with partially overlapping sink sets. The fundamental tension this exposes is that cache invalidation granularity in current systems (vLLM, SGLang) is at the level of entire prefix blocks (typically 16-32 tokens per page), so even a theoretically sound invalidation criterion that correctly identifies a single divergent sink position forces eviction of the entire block — a coarse hammer that may discard mostly-valid KV entries, suggesting that finer-grained per-token validity bits within cache pages would be needed to make selective invalidation economically worthwhile.
